blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes an experience report from a 2014 University of Maryland course where undergraduates learned to program smart contracts. The paper highlights the unique challenges of smart contract development compared to traditional software, emphasizing the need for an 'economic thinking' perspective to ensure fairness and security. The authors illustrate three common classes of mistakes students made when implementing a simple 'Rock, Paper, Scissors' game: leaking money due to logical errors in state machine encoding, hiding inputs in plain sight by failing to use cryptographic commitments, and misaligned incentives where players could exploit the contract's design. The blog post underscores how even trivial smart contracts are prone to subtle bugs and require rigorous scrutiny, combining skills from verification, concurrency, cryptography, cybersecurity, and game theory. It also notes Ethereum-specific pitfalls like call-stack limits and transaction-ordering dependencies.
paper_title: Step by step towards creating a safe smart contract: lessons and insights from a cryptocurrency lab
paper_abstract: We document our experiences in teaching smart contract programming to undergraduate students at the University of Maryland, the first pedagogical attempt of its kind. Since smart contracts deal directly with the movement of valuable currency units between contratual parties, security of a contract program is of paramount importance. Our lab exposed numerous common pitfalls in designing safe and secure smart contracts. We document several typical classes of mistakes students made, suggest ways to fix/avoid them, and advocate best practices for programming smart contracts. Finally, our pedagogical efforts have also resulted in online open course materials for programming smart contracts, which may be of independent interest to the community.

figures.title: Schematic of a decentralized cryptocurrency system with smart contracts
figures.caption: Schematic of a decentralized cryptocurrency system with smart contracts. A smart contract’s state is stored on the public blockchain. A smart contract program is executed by a network of miners who reach consensus on the outcome of the execution, and update the contract’s state on the blockchain accordingly. Users can send money or data to a contract; or receive money or data from a contract.
